notes: User is grieving a loved grandmother and remains in a difficult but hopeful healing period. They attended five bereavement support sessions last year; the kind facilitator, members with similar experiences, and judgment-free community helped them process emotions and feel less alone. They are considering reconnecting with the facilitator/group, finding a therapist or counselor, exploring grief/mental-health forums or communities, and reaching out to friends or family with similar lived experience. Writing/journaling has long been therapeutic, and they plan to start a journal for emotional processing and clarity. They are also organizing a memory box for their grandmother, already including her locket and handwritten recipe book; they may add objects, photos, stories, and family contributions over time, preserving fragile/archival items thoughtfully. To rebuild routine, they chose 10–15 minutes of bodyweight exercise three times weekly, with small goals and progress tracking. They are resuming reading, especially memoirs, beginning with Cheryl Strayed’s “Wild,” and may read Brené Brown’s “Daring Greatly.” Respond with empathy and gentle pacing; avoid assumptions about dates, beliefs

Offer practical, personalized suggestions for arranging, preserving, and caring for fragile or archival items, as well as ways to periodically revisit the box, add new memories, tell stories, and potentially digitize contents. Avoid assumptions about dates, losses, beliefs, or preferred rituals.
